title: the summit sit
hook: a king without a kingdom and a merchant without a family sit in a forest and ask a sage the same question

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground, and the last stop on this year's walk through the regions. Did you notice a place where more than one way of praying shares the same ground? Today the climbing stops for a while. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.
screen: `PUNJAB'S SHARED DEVOTIONAL GROUND.` · `THE CLIMBING STOPS FOR A WHILE.`

segments.voice: A forest hermitage. A king sits on the ground. His ministers turned on him and his enemies took his city, and he's lost everything. Beside him sits a merchant whose own wife and sons threw him out of the house for his money. Here's the strange part. The king keeps worrying about his old elephants and his treasury. The merchant keeps wondering whether his family is well. They both know these thoughts make no sense. So they ask the sage of the hermitage: why can't the mind let go? That's where this year began, many months ago. Today's summit sit goes back to that forest.
screen: `A KING WITHOUT A KINGDOM.` → `A MERCHANT WITHOUT A FAMILY.` → `WHY CAN'T THE MIND LET GO?`

segments.voice: First, the name of these days. A summit sit is a stop near the top of the year. The path has climbed a long way: the goddess, Shiva, the schools of thought, the Vedas, the women of the epics, the regions. For the next stretch, each day stands on the top and looks back down at one part of the climb, then sits with it. No new trail. Just the view. Start where the year started, with the Devi Mahatmya. The king is Suratha. The merchant is Samadhi. The sage is Medhas. And his answer to their question is the whole book. The pull they feel, he says, is the work of the goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that draws the minds of even the wise into confusion. Then he tells them who she is, through her stories: the goddess leaving the sleeping Vishnu so that he wakes to face two demons, the goddess given every god's weapon to face the buffalo demon Mahisha, and the goddess who meets Shumbha and Nishumbha, with Kali springing from her brow. The same power that binds the mind, Medhas says, is the power that sets it free. And the book doesn't end on a battlefield. It ends by a river. The king and the merchant go there, worship the goddess, and she appears and asks what each of them wants. The king asks for his kingdom back, and she grants it. The merchant, the man whose family drove him out, asks for something else: the knowledge that loosens the grip of me and mine. She grants that too. Same forest, same question, same goddess, and two different answers. The question the book opens with is a very ordinary one. Why does my mind keep going back to what hurt me? The book doesn't scold the question. It builds a whole scripture around it.
screen: `A SUMMIT SIT: ONE STRETCH, SEEN FROM THE TOP.` · `THE KING, THE MERCHANT AND THE SAGE.` · `THE POWER THAT BINDS IS THE POWER THAT FREES.` · `A KINGDOM BACK, OR A LOOSENED GRIP.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS NOT SCOLDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the king's question, asked gently. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Then notice one thing your mind keeps going back to, the way the king went back to his elephants. Don't argue with it, and don't follow it. Just name it once, quietly, and let it sit next to you like the merchant sat next to the king. Each time it pulls, come back to the breath. If you pray, you can hold it up to the goddess, or to God, the way the two of them did by the river. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. A stop near the top of the year, looking back at one stretch. Today's stretch: the Devi Mahatmya, and the question of a king and a merchant. Today's word.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, when your mind goes back to an old hurt, ask the king's question once, kindly: why do I keep coming back here? Then let it be a question. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Some devotees of the goddess recite the Devi Mahatmya in full, in one sitting or spread across the nights of Navaratri.

notes: First day of 'the summit sit' (1412–1424 in the outline, under 'Festivals held; year close').
